lead: Speech sits near 0 Hz, and a wire or an antenna will not carry it far. Modulation lifts the message onto a high-frequency carrier — a steady sine wave — by varying that carrier's amplitude, frequency or phase in step with the message. The same three knobs carry bits, giving ASK, FSK and PSK. Every telephone modem, TV tower, Wi-Fi chip and optical link does this. This chapter covers analog forms AM, FM and PM, then the digital forms, ending at QAM where baud rate and bit rate part company.
prereq: You need: 2.1 for amplitude, frequency and phase, 2.3 for bandwidth and capacity, and 2.4 for what a band-pass medium does to a signal.

sections.h3: Why a signal needs a carrier

blocks.text: A baseband signal — a voice, a bit stream — holds most of its energy near 0 Hz. Many media do not pass 0 Hz. A radio channel, a cable TV plant, a telephone line with a transformer: each passes only a band of frequencies around some centre frequency. That kind of path is a band-pass channel. Push baseband into it and nothing useful comes out.

Modulation solves this. Take a carrier, the sine wave A<sub>c</sub> cos(2πf<sub>c</sub>t), where A<sub>c</sub> is the carrier peak amplitude in volts, f<sub>c</sub> the carrier frequency in hertz, and t time in seconds. Vary one parameter of that carrier in step with the message. The message now rides inside the band the channel passes.

A second reason is the antenna. An antenna radiates well when its length is about a quarter wavelength, λ/4, with λ = c/f and c = 3 × 10<sup>8</sup> m/s. A 1 kHz tone has λ = 300 km, so λ/4 = 75 km — useless. At 100 MHz, λ = 3 m and λ/4 = 75 cm. Shifting the signal up in frequency makes it radiate.
A third reason: many signals can share one medium by sitting on different carriers. That is frequency-division multiplexing (FDM), and 2.7 builds on it.
In AM the carrier amplitude follows the message. For a single tone the wave is:

blocks.where: A<sub>c</sub> is the carrier peak amplitude in V, f<sub>c</sub> the carrier frequency in Hz, f<sub>m</sub> the message frequency in Hz, t time in s, and μ = A<sub>m</sub>/A<sub>c</sub> the modulation index (no units), with A<sub>m</sub> the message peak amplitude in V.

blocks.text: The square bracket is the envelope. It swings between A<sub>c</sub>(1 + μ) and A<sub>c</sub>(1 − μ). Multiplying the two cosines gives three frequencies: the carrier f<sub>c</sub> and two sidebands at f<sub>c</sub> − f<sub>m</sub> and f<sub>c</sub> + f<sub>m</sub>. So a single tone occupies 2f<sub>m</sub> Hz. A message band reaching f<sub>m(max)</sub> takes 2f<sub>m(max)</sub> Hz.

Keep μ ≤ 1. At μ = 1 the envelope just touches zero. Past that — overmodulation — the envelope crosses over, the phase flips for part of each cycle, and the recovered audio inverts and distorts. More depth is not more loudness; it is a broken signal.

The carrier itself carries no information; it is a pure sine. DSB-SC (double-sideband suppressed carrier) removes it and saves power. SSB-SC (single-sideband suppressed carrier) also removes one sideband, halving the bandwidth to f<sub>m</sub>, which is why shortwave radio uses it.

In FM the instantaneous frequency is f<sub>c</sub> + k<sub>f</sub>m(t), where k<sub>f</sub> is the frequency sensitivity in Hz/V and m(t) the message in volts. For a tone of peak amplitude A<sub>m</sub>, the peak frequency deviation is Δf = k<sub>f</sub>A<sub>m</sub> Hz. The FM modulation index is β = Δf/f<sub>m</sub>, a pure number.

blocks.where: B is the practical FM bandwidth in Hz, Δf the peak frequency deviation in Hz, f<sub>m</sub> the highest message frequency in Hz (Carson's rule).

blocks.text: In PM it is the phase that shifts, by an amount proportional to m(t); the index is the peak phase deviation in radians. FM and PM waves have a constant envelope, so amplitude noise is stripped by a limiter before detection — that is their noise immunity. The price is bandwidth: with β = 5, Carson gives B ≈ 12f<sub>m</sub>, twelve times the message bandwidth.

sections.h3: Digital modulation: ASK, FSK, PSK, QAM

blocks.text: Digital modulation uses the same three knobs, driven by bits instead of a voice.

ASK switches the carrier amplitude between levels. When one level is zero it is on-off keying (OOK). Noise adds straight to amplitude, so ASK is fragile. ASK is fragile, but it is cheap: a light source switched fully on and off is an ASK signal, which is why on-off keying suits optical fibre links.
FSK jumps the carrier between two frequencies (BFSK). The envelope stays constant, so clipping and amplitude distortion do not matter; bandwidth is wider than ASK.

PSK switches phase. BPSK uses two phases 180° apart, giving 1 bit per symbol. Those two symbols are as far apart as two points on a circle can be, so noise must be large to push one symbol into the other; of ASK, FSK and PSK, BPSK gives the fewest bit errors for the same signal-to-noise ratio. QPSK uses four phases 90° apart, giving 2 bits per symbol in the same bandwidth.

QAM varies amplitude and phase together, placing M points in a constellation — a plot of the two carrier components. QAM-16 is a 4 × 4 grid, 4 bits per symbol; QAM-64 is an 8 × 8 grid, 6 bits per symbol. More points mean closer neighbours, so a higher QAM needs a cleaner channel (see 2.2).

blocks.where: R<sub>b</sub> is the bit rate in bit/s, R<sub>s</sub> the symbol (baud) rate in symbols/s, and M the number of constellation states.

blocks.text: The box that does all this at both ends is the modem: modulator on send, demodulator on receive.

figure.caption: Bits become voltages, the modulator multiplies them by the carrier, the band-pass channel passes only the band around the carrier, and the demodulator takes the carrier back out.

spec.title: A modem link
spec.aria: A one-way chain: bits, line coder, modulator multiplying by the carrier, channel, demodulator, bits out.

examples.question: A 1 kHz tone with peak amplitude 6 V amplitude-modulates a 100 kHz carrier of peak amplitude 10 V. Find the modulation index, the two sideband frequencies, the bandwidth and the peak amplitude of the AM wave. A QAM-16 modem with a symbol rate of 2400 baud; find its bit rate.
steps: Data: f<sub>m</sub> = 1 kHz, A<sub>m</sub> = 6 V, f<sub>c</sub> = 100 kHz, A<sub>c</sub> = 10 V.
μ = 0.6 ≤ 1, so there is no overmodulation.
Peak amplitude of the wave: A<sub>c</sub>(1 + μ) = 10 × 1.6 = 16 V; its minimum is 10 × 0.4 = 4 V.
QAM-16 carries log₂16 = 4 bits per symbol.
examples.answer: μ = 0.6 (60%) with no overmodulation, sidebands at 99 kHz and 101 kHz, bandwidth 2 kHz, peak amplitude 16 V (minimum 4 V), and the QAM-16 modem delivers 4 bits per symbol at 9600 bit/s.
examples.check:
import math
Am = 6.0
Ac = 10.0
fm = 1e3
fc = 100e3
mu = Am/Ac
print(mu)
print((fc-fm)/1e3)
print((fc+fm)/1e3)
print(2*fm/1e3)
print(Ac*(1+mu))
print(Ac*(1-mu))
M = 16
bps = math.log2(M)
print(bps)
print(2400*bps)

examples.question: A QAM-64 modem runs at 2000 baud over a clean link. Find its bit rate.
examples.answer: The bit rate is 12000 bit/s, i.e. 12 kbit/s.
examples.check:
import math
Rs = 2000
M = 64
bps = math.log2(M)
print(bps)
print(Rs*bps)

traps: μ > 1 is not deeper modulation. Past 100% the envelope crosses over and the audio inverts and distorts.
Bit rate is baud rate × log₂M, not baud rate × M. QAM-16 at 2400 baud is 9600 bit/s, not 38400 bit/s.
For a single-tone AM wave the bandwidth is 2f<sub>m</sub>, not f<sub>m</sub>. The f<sub>m</sub> figure belongs to single sideband.
In FM, Δf is the peak frequency deviation, not the bandwidth. Carson's rule adds Δf and f<sub>m</sub> before doubling.
Do not swap f<sub>c</sub> and f<sub>m</sub>: the sidebands are f<sub>c</sub> ± f<sub>m</sub>, so the carrier is the larger number in an AM radio link.

quiz.q: Define the AM modulation index and state the condition for no overmodulation.
quiz.a: μ = A<sub>m</sub>/A<sub>c</sub>, the message peak amplitude divided by the carrier peak amplitude. No overmodulation when μ ≤ 1.

quiz.q: Why does the carrier of an AM wave carry no information?
quiz.a: It is a fixed sine at f<sub>c</sub> with constant amplitude; all message-dependent variation sits in the two sidebands. Removing it — DSB-SC — leaves the message recoverable.

quiz.q: Why does FM resist noise better than AM, and what does it pay for that?
quiz.a: FM carries the message in frequency and keeps a constant envelope, so amplitude noise is removed by a limiter before detection. It pays in bandwidth: Carson's rule gives B ≈ 2(Δf + f<sub>m</sub>), which is many times the message bandwidth.

quiz.q: A 2 kHz tone with peak amplitude 4 V modulates a 200 kHz carrier of peak amplitude 8 V. Find μ, the sidebands, the bandwidth and the peak amplitude.
quiz.a: μ = 4 ÷ 8 = 0.5. Sidebands at 200 − 2 = 198 kHz and 200 + 2 = 202 kHz. Bandwidth = 4 kHz = 2f<sub>m</sub>. Peak amplitude = 8 × 1.5 = 12 V.

quiz.q: A QAM-16 modem transmits 3000 symbols per second. Find its bit rate.
quiz.a: log₂16 = 4 bits per symbol, so bit rate = 3000 × 4 = 12000 bit/s.

quiz.q: An operator drives an AM transmitter to μ = 1.4 to 'get more power across'. Explain what a listener actually hears.
quiz.a: The envelope passes through zero and crosses over for part of each cycle, so the phase inverts. The envelope detector folds the waveform and the recovered audio is distorted and partly inverted. Overmodulation produces splatter into neighbouring channels, not more loudness.

quiz.q: Why does QAM-64 need a cleaner channel than QAM-16 at the same peak amplitude?
quiz.a: QAM-64 puts 64 points into the same peak swing, so neighbouring points are closer than in the 16-point grid. The same noise voltage is more likely to push a symbol across a decision boundary, so a higher signal-to-noise ratio is needed to hold the bit error rate.

beyond: Not for the exam. Wi-Fi runs QAM-64 up to QAM-1024 with OFDM, and LTE goes to 256-QAM; the constellation diagram is a live diagnostic in every radio lab, where error-vector magnitude (EVM) measures how far received symbols sit from their ideal points. Software-defined radios let you change the scheme in code rather than hardware. Search for constellation diagram, EVM, and peak-to-average power ratio (PAPR) to go further.
